sections.content: You know *imprimido* and *impreso*, *freído* and *frito*, *proveído* and *provisto* from B2 Unit 20. Here the question is the norm in formal writing. After *haber* and in the *ser* passive, both forms are valid for all three verbs. When the participle is an adjective (next to a noun or after *estar*), the verbs differ. *Freír* takes almost only *frito*, and *pescado freído* is the one real error. *Imprimir* has *impreso* as the preferred form in formal writing, but *imprimido* is not wrong. *Proveer* accepts both, with *provisto* the usual one.

sections.title: Where each form can go
rows: La imprenta ha imprimido mil ejemplares.
The printing house has printed a thousand copies. (haber: long form)
La imprenta ha impreso mil ejemplares.
The printing house has printed a thousand copies. (haber: short form)
A printed manual. (adjective: impreso preferred in formal writing, imprimido not wrong)
A printing house supplied with paper. (adjective: both valid, provista usual)

items.spanish: La biblioteca está provista de diccionarios.
items.english: The library is supplied with dictionaries.

items.spanish: La redacción ha provisto de manuales a los correctores.
items.english: The editorial office has supplied the proofreaders with style guides.

sections.content: English uses one form for everything (*printed*, *fried*), so nothing warns you to switch. Keep one fixed point: when the participle describes fried food, write *frito*, never *freído*. For the other two verbs, write the short form (*impreso*, *provisto*) when the participle describes a noun and the register is formal. The long form is not an error there, only less usual.
